entry.title: Reaching a localhost AI agent from anywhere, without port forwarding or client apps
entry.content:
I run a coding agent on my laptop. It holds my repositories, credentials, and tools, and its web UI binds to 127.0.0.1. That default is correct security, and it also leaves the agent unreachable the moment I step away. I made the agent, and the desktop it runs on, reachable from any browser with no ports opened to the internet, nothing installed on the devices I connect from, and every request authenticated before it reaches the machine.

Context and requirements

The agent runs arbitrary commands with my privileges, so exposing its UI is exposing a shell. Remote access is a security problem before it is a convenience.

  • Browser-only clients. A phone or borrowed laptop needs nothing beyond a browser.
  • Authentication before the origin. Unauthenticated requests never reach the laptop, not even the agent's login page.
  • No inbound exposure. No port-forwarding, no public IP; the services I add listen on loopback only.
  • Remote desktop. Some workflows need the full GUI, not just the web UI.
  • Explicit lifecycle. I start and stop the stack deliberately; it is not a login daemon.

Non-goals: multi-user access, high availability, and use while the laptop is asleep or offline.

Design

Three layers: an outbound tunnel from the laptop to an edge network, an identity gate at that edge, and local services that stay on loopback.

flowchart LR
    B["Browser<br/>(phone or laptop)"] -->|HTTPS| E["Edge network"]
    subgraph Edge
        E --> A["Identity gate<br/>(per-hostname policy)"]
    end
    A -->|"existing outbound connection"| C["Tunnel connector<br/>(on the laptop)"]
    subgraph Laptop
        C --> AG["Agent web UI<br/>127.0.0.1:3000"]
        C --> WS["WebSocket→VNC bridge<br/>127.0.0.1:6080"]
        WS --> VNC["OS screen sharing<br/>:5900 (all interfaces)"]
    end
  • Tunnel connector. Opens outbound connections to the edge, which routes each hostname down to a local service. Nothing accepts inbound traffic.
  • Identity gate. Each hostname has an edge access policy. Requests without a session are redirected to a login flow and only forwarded once it passes.
  • Local services. The agent's web UI on 127.0.0.1:3000, and a WebSocket-to-VNC bridge on 127.0.0.1:6080 in front of the built-in screen-sharing server.

The laptop sees nothing until the identity check succeeds:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant E as Edge + identity gate
    participant C as Tunnel connector
    participant S as Local service
    B->>E: GET https://agent.example.com
    E-->>B: 302 → login (no session)
    B->>E: Email one-time code
    E-->>B: Session cookie
    B->>E: GET https://agent.example.com
    E->>C: Forward over existing outbound connection
    C->>S: http://127.0.0.1:3000
    S-->>C: Response
    C-->>E: Response
    E-->>B: Response

Routing is one declarative table:

ingress:
  - hostname: agent.example.com
    service: http://127.0.0.1:3000
  - hostname: desk.example.com
    service: http://127.0.0.1:6080
  - service: http_status:404   # anything not listed above fails closed

The catch-all matters: a hostname pointed at the tunnel by mistake returns 404 instead of reaching a service.

Decisions

Decision Chosen Alternatives considered Why
Transport Cloudflare Tunnel Port-forwarding, Tailscale (incl. Funnel), ngrok Outbound-only; tunnels, DNS, and policies live in one account with one CLI; WebSockets pass through. Costs a domain, and Cloudflare terminates TLS at its edge.
Authentication Cloudflare Access, email one-time code App-level password, IP allow-list, VPN The check happens before a request reaches the machine; sessions expire and revoke centrally. No shared password, so your email becomes the root of trust.
Remote desktop Built-in screen sharing (VNC) + noVNC Guacamole, MeshCentral, RustDesk OS-native, so no screen-recording permission for a third party, with a tiny stack. VNC auth alone is weak, and macOS ignores remote resizing.
Lifecycle On-demand start/stop script launchd / systemd Exposure stays a deliberate choice, not a permanent property of the machine. The cost is that a crash stays down until I notice.

The agent's own host allow-list stays enabled behind all of this as a second layer.

Security posture

  • The agent and the bridge bind to 127.0.0.1; from the internet, the tunnel is the only path in.
  • macOS Screen Sharing listens on port 5900 on all interfaces and cannot be restricted to loopback. It is reachable on the local network but not the internet. I limit it to my account, rely on Apple Remote Desktop authentication, and keep the firewall on.
  • Every routed hostname has a policy; unrouted hostnames fail closed at the connector.
  • The tunnel credential lives in a mode-0600 file and is passed with --token-file, so it never appears in process listings or shell history.

Residual risks: compromise of the email account, reliance on Cloudflare as an intermediary, the Screen Sharing listener on shared Wi-Fi, and an unlocked desktop anyone with physical access can use. Hardening I still want: validate the Access token and audience at the connector so an unpolicied hostname fails closed, and shorten the desktop session duration.

Running it unattended

On demand is the default, but three things let it run unattended: the laptop must not sleep (sudo pmset -a sleep 0 displaysleep 0 disksleep 0), it must stay logged in with auto-lock off so the desktop shows instead of the lock screen, and the lid stays open (clamshell with an external display also works). To start the stack on boot, load the same script under launchd or systemd with RunAtLoad, or keep caffeinate in a login item. The trade-off is unchanged: an always-on, always-unlocked desktop is a bigger target, so leave it up only where the machine is physically secure.

What broke along the way

  1. The agent rejected the public hostname. Its web server validates Host and Origin headers, a DNS-rebinding defense, and answered Untrusted request. Rewriting Host at the connector would have broken the UI's own same-origin checks. The fix was to add the public hostname to the application's allow-list.
  2. Enabling Access through the API left no login method. The dashboard adds a one-time-code provider for you; the API does not. The login page reported "no login methods available" until I created it explicitly.
  3. noVNC asked for a username. macOS advertises Apple Remote Desktop authentication first, so noVNC expects the macOS account, not the VNC password. I briefly patched the client to prefer VNC auth, then reverted it to keep the checkout upstream-clean.
  4. The desktop cannot be resized. macOS ignores client resize requests. Scale client-side in noVNC (resize=scale) or lower the display resolution.
  5. Restarting the agent from inside the agent ends the session. The restart shell is a child of the process it kills. Change the agent's server from a separate terminal.
  6. launchd services do not inherit the shell's PATH. Homebrew binaries need absolute paths, one more reason to use an explicit script.

Result

agent.example.com and desk.example.com resolve to the edge. After an email one-time code, they reach the agent UI and the desktop. The laptop runs three processes, the tunnel connector, the VNC bridge, and the agent, and accepts no inbound connections from the internet.

The step-by-step setup, with verification and teardown, is in the companion guide.

entry.title: Browser access to a local agent and desktop with Cloudflare Tunnel and Access
entry.content:
This is the operational companion to Reaching a localhost AI agent from anywhere. It covers prerequisites, ordered steps with a verification after each, troubleshooting, and teardown.

Placeholders: example.com for your domain, agent.example.com and desk.example.com for the two hostnames, you@example.com for your login email, and 127.0.0.1:3000 for the agent's web UI.

Prerequisites

  • A domain whose DNS is active on Cloudflare.
  • cloudflared on the laptop (brew install cloudflared).
  • The Cloudflare CLI, cf (npm install --global cf; requires Node.js 22.18 or later). It was in beta at the time of writing, so check --help if a flag has changed.
  • jq, for parsing CLI output.
  • An agent web UI bound to 127.0.0.1:3000.
  • macOS, for the remote-desktop portion.

Ordering matters. Create the access policies before the tunnel connector runs, so there is never a window in which a hostname is routable but unauthenticated.

1. Authenticate the CLI

cf auth login                       # browser-based device authorization
cf zones list --name example.com    # confirm the zone exists and is active

2. Enable Access and a login method

Creating the Zero Trust organization through the API does not add a login method, so add the one-time-code identity provider explicitly.

cf zero-trust organization create --body '{"name":"personal"}'
cf zero-trust identity-providers create \
  --body '{"name":"Email OTP","type":"onetimepin","config":{}}'

Verify: cf zero-trust identity-providers list shows a provider of type onetimepin.

3. Create an access policy per hostname

for host in agent desk; do
  cf zero-trust access applications create --body "$(jq -nc --arg d "$host.example.com" '{
    name: $d, domain: $d, type: "self_hosted", session_duration: "24h",
    policies: [{ name: "owner", decision: "allow",
                 include: [{ email: { email: "you@example.com" } }] }]
  }')"
done

4. Create the tunnel, routes, and DNS records

TUNNEL_ID=$(cf tunnels create --name laptop --config-source cloudflare | jq -r .id)

cf tunnels config update "$TUNNEL_ID" --body '{
  "config": { "ingress": [
    { "hostname": "agent.example.com", "service": "http://127.0.0.1:3000" },
    { "hostname": "desk.example.com",  "service": "http://127.0.0.1:6080" },
    { "service": "http_status:404" }
  ]}
}'

for host in agent desk; do
  cf dns records create --zone example.com --body "$(jq -nc \
    --arg n "$host" --arg t "$TUNNEL_ID.cfargotunnel.com" \
    '{type: "CNAME", name: $n, content: $t, proxied: true}')"
done

Store the connector token in a file readable only by you. Passing it with --token-file later keeps it out of process listings and shell history.

install -d -m 700 ~/.cloudflared
cf tunnels token get "$TUNNEL_ID" | jq -r . > ~/.cloudflared/laptop.token
chmod 600 ~/.cloudflared/laptop.token

5. Allow the public hostname in the agent

Many local web UIs validate the Host and Origin headers to block DNS rebinding. If yours does, it will reject agent.example.com until you add that hostname to its allow-list. The setting is tool-specific. It is usually an environment variable or a config key. Do not work around it by rewriting the Host header at the connector; that breaks same-origin checks for the UI's API calls.

6. Enable screen sharing and the browser bridge

In System Settings → General → Sharing, turn on Screen Sharing and limit Allow access for to your account. Screen Sharing listens on port 5900 on every network interface, not only loopback, so it is reachable from your local network. Keep the macOS firewall on, and avoid leaving it enabled on shared or public Wi-Fi.

Then install the browser client and the WebSocket bridge:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/novnc/noVNC ~/remote-access/noVNC
python3 -m pip install --user websockify

When you connect, noVNC prompts for a username and password. Those are your macOS account credentials, not a VNC password, because macOS offers Apple Remote Desktop authentication first.

7. Add a start/stop script

The agent keeps its own lifecycle. This script manages only the bridge and the tunnel connector. Save it as remote somewhere on your PATH.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# remote: start, stop, and inspect the remote-access stack on demand
set -u
RUN="$HOME/remote-access/run"
mkdir -p "$RUN"

start() {
  nohup websockify --web="$HOME/remote-access/noVNC" 127.0.0.1:6080 127.0.0.1:5900 \
    > "$RUN/novnc.log" 2>&1 &
  echo $! > "$RUN/novnc.pid"

  nohup cloudflared tunnel run --token-file "$HOME/.cloudflared/laptop.token" \
    > "$RUN/tunnel.log" 2>&1 &
  echo $! > "$RUN/tunnel.pid"
}

stop() {
  for f in "$RUN"/*.pid; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    kill "$(cat "$f")" 2>/dev/null
    rm -f "$f"
  done
}

status() {
  for f in "$RUN"/*.pid; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    name=$(basename "$f" .pid)
    if kill -0 "$(cat "$f")" 2>/dev/null; then echo "$name: up"; else echo "$name: down"; fi
  done
}

case "${1:-status}" in
  start)  start ;;
  stop)   stop ;;
  status) status ;;
  *)      echo "usage: remote {start|stop|status}" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

pip install --user places websockify under ~/Library/Python/<version>/bin. Add that directory to your PATH or use the absolute path in the script.

8. Verify

remote start
cf tunnels list | jq '.[] | {name, status}'                     # expect "healthy"
curl -sI https://agent.example.com | grep -iE '^(HTTP|location)'
# expect: HTTP/2 302 and a location under <team>.cloudflareaccess.com

The 302 to the Access login page is the most important check: it shows that unauthenticated requests stop at the edge.

Then, in a browser:

  • https://agent.example.com → email one-time code → the agent UI.
  • https://desk.example.com/vnc.html?autoconnect=1&resize=scale → email one-time code → the desktop, scaled to the window.

9. Run it unattended

Keep the laptop awake and logged in so it keeps serving:

sudo pmset -a sleep 0 displaysleep 0 disksleep 0

Set Lock Screen → Require password after screen saver begins or display is turned off to Never, so the desktop shows instead of a lock screen. Keep the lid open and the laptop on power; closing the lid puts it to sleep regardless, unless it is in clamshell mode with an external display. Revert with sudo pmset restoredefaults.

To make the stack start on boot, install the remote start command as a user agent:

# ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.remote.plist
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.example.remote</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array><string>/usr/local/bin/remote</string><string>start</string></array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
</dict>
</plist>
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.remote.plist

Or keep it on demand and run caffeinate -dimsu in a login item to block sleep while you leave it up. Either way, remember the trade-off: an always-on, always-unlocked desktop is a bigger target, so leave it unattended only where the machine is physically secure.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause Fix
"There are no login methods available" No identity provider configured Step 2
Untrusted request from the agent Host allow-list in the agent Step 5
noVNC asks for a username macOS offers Apple Remote Desktop auth first Use your macOS account credentials
Desktop is too large to read macOS ignores remote resize requests resize=scale, or lower the display resolution
Tunnel shows inactive Connector is not running remote status; check ~/remote-access/run/tunnel.log
Lock screen instead of the desktop Auto-lock is enabled Step 9

Teardown

remote stop

for host in agent desk; do
  id=$(cf dns records list --zone example.com --name "$host.example.com" | jq -r '.[0].id')
  cf dns records delete "$id" --zone example.com
done

cf tunnels delete "$TUNNEL_ID"
rm -f ~/.cloudflared/laptop.token

Finally, delete the two Access applications (cf zero-trust access applications delete <app-id>), turn off Screen Sharing, and restore your power and lock-screen settings.

entry.title: Homebrew: Remove a Formula and Its Unused Dependencies
entry.content:
Large formulae pull in a lot of dependencies. At the time of writing, ffmpeg depended on more than 30 other formulae, many with dependencies of their own. brew uninstall ffmpeg removes ffmpeg and leaves all of them behind.

brew info ffmpeg
# ==> Dependencies
# Build: nasm, pkg-config
# Required: aom, dav1d, fontconfig, freetype, frei0r, gnutls, lame, libass, ...

The short answer

Since Homebrew 2.5.9 (late 2020), the built-in way is:

brew uninstall ffmpeg
brew autoremove --dry-run   # review what would be removed
brew autoremove

autoremove uninstalls formulae that were installed only as dependencies and that nothing else installed still needs. It reads Homebrew's own record of what you asked for (installed_on_request) and what came along as a dependency, so it won't remove a dependency that another formula still uses, or one you installed directly.

The older one-liner

Before autoremove, the common approach looked like this. I originally published it in this post:

pkg=ffmpeg
brew uninstall "$pkg"
brew uninstall $(join <(brew leaves) <(brew deps "$pkg"))

How it works:

  1. brew deps "$pkg" lists the formula's dependencies.
  2. brew leaves lists installed formulae that no other installed formula depends on.
  3. join keeps the names in both lists: dependencies of pkg that are now leaves, so nothing else needs them.

It works for simple cases but has sharp edges:

  • It can remove things you meant to keep. brew leaves includes formulae you installed on purpose. If you installed pkg-config yourself, it is still a leaf and still a dependency of ffmpeg, so it gets removed. autoremove knows the difference.
  • It only cleans up one level. Sub-dependencies become leaves only after their parents are removed, so you have to run it repeatedly.
  • join assumes sorted input. Both commands happen to print sorted output today; nothing guarantees it.

Use brew autoremove, and pass --dry-run first whenever you're unsure.

entry.title: Fixing the CSS Integrity Digest Error in Hugo
entry.content:
Symptom

The deployed site renders as unstyled HTML, while hugo server looks fine locally. The browser console shows:

Failed to find a valid digest in the 'integrity' attribute for resource '…/style.min..css'
with computed SHA-256 integrity '…'. The resource has been blocked.

Why it happens

Many Hugo themes use Subresource Integrity (SRI). At build time, Hugo fingerprints the stylesheet and writes its hash into the page:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ $style.Permalink }}" integrity="{{ $style.Data.Integrity }}" crossorigin="anonymous">

The browser hashes the file it actually downloads and refuses to apply it if the two hashes differ. So this error always means one thing: the bytes the browser received are not the bytes Hugo hashed. Something between the build and the browser changed the file.

Cause 1: a CDN rewrote the file

If the site sits behind Cloudflare, its optimizations could modify assets in transit:

  • Auto Minify (retired by Cloudflare in August 2024) re-minified CSS and JavaScript, which changes the bytes and breaks the hash.
  • Rocket Loader rewrites how scripts load.

Disable these optimizations for the site, then purge the cache (Caching → Configuration → Purge Everything, or purge just the affected URLs). Cached copies keep failing until they expire or are purged.

Cause 2: line endings changed in Git

If the theme or its assets were committed from different operating systems, Git can convert line endings (LF ↔ CRLF). The file in the build environment then differs from the one that was fingerprinted elsewhere. This was the confirmed fix for several people in the Anatole theme thread.

Normalize line endings for the repository:

# macOS / Linux: convert CRLF to LF on commit, never on checkout
git config --global core.autocrlf input
# Windows: check out CRLF, commit LF
git config --global core.autocrlf true

Then re-normalize the files already in the repository:

git add --renormalize .
git commit -m "Normalize line endings"

A committed .gitattributes file (for example, * text=auto eol=lf) is more reliable than per-machine settings, because it travels with the repository. See GitHub's guide on configuring Git to handle line endings.

Cause 3 (last resort): remove the integrity check

If you can't find what is modifying the file, you can remove the integrity attribute from the theme's template, usually in layouts/_default/baseof.html or a head partial:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ $style.Permalink }}">

This makes the error go away by turning off the check, not by fixing the cause. SRI matters most for files served from a third-party CDN; for a stylesheet served from your own origin, removing it is a smaller risk. Prefer fixing causes 1 and 2.

References

  • Subresource Integrity, MDN
  • Configuring Git to handle line endings, GitHub Docs
  • Valid digest integrity issue, Anatole theme
  • SHA-256 integrity issue, hugo-theme-bootstrap4-blog

entry.title: Workshop Prep: Building a Personal Site with Hugo
entry.content:
This post accompanied the ACM Luther workshop "Building a Personal Static Website" on October 18, 2020. The commands have been updated to work today.

Why a static site generator

Hugo is a fast, open-source static site generator. You write content in Markdown, Hugo renders it to plain HTML, and you can host the result almost anywhere for free. In the workshop we built a personal portfolio and published it on GitHub Pages; the workshop example site is still online.

Before the workshop, set up Git and install Hugo.

Step 1: Git and GitHub

The workshop uses only a handful of Git commands:

git status
git add <path>
git commit -m "Describe your change"
git push origin main

If Git is new to you, GitHub's Git cheat sheet is a good one-page reference.

  1. Create a GitHub account if you don't have one.
  2. Install Git:
    • Windows: Git for Windows
    • macOS: run git --version; if Git isn't installed, macOS offers to install the Command Line Tools.
    • Ubuntu / Debian: sudo apt install git
  3. Set your name and email. Git records them on every commit.
git config --global user.name "Jane Doe"
git config --global user.email jane@example.com
  1. Generate an SSH key and add it to your GitHub account, so you can push without typing a password.

Step 2: Install Hugo

Follow the official installation guide for your platform. The common options:

# macOS (Homebrew, from https://brew.sh)
brew install hugo

# Windows (winget)
winget install Hugo.Hugo.Extended

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install hugo

Many themes need the extended edition of Hugo for Sass support. The Homebrew and winget packages are extended; distribution packages may lag behind, so check the version.

Step 3: Verify

hugo version
# hugo v0.xxx.x+extended ...

If that prints a version, you're ready for the workshop.

Prepared by Swopnil Shrestha for ACM Luther's 2020–21 workshop series.

entry.title: Building a toy VPN: cipher negotiation, Diffie-Hellman, and HMAC from first principles
entry.content:
A VPN makes two machines on an untrusted network behave as if they were on a private link: an observer on the path can see that traffic is flowing, but cannot read or modify it. For Luther College's CS-460 (Information Assurance and Security), I built the core of that idea as a small Python client and server. The code is on GitHub.

It is not a VPN you should use. It has no routing or tunnel interface, and the cryptography has real flaws, which I list at the end. But building the handshake by hand is the fastest way I know to understand why production protocols look the way they do.

The protocol

A session has three phases: agree on a cipher, agree on a key, and exchange messages.

1. Cipher negotiation

The client sends the algorithms and key sizes it supports. The server intersects that list with its own and picks the strongest common option.

client → ProposedCiphers:AES:[128,192,256],Blowfish:[112,224,448],DES:[56]
server → ChosenCipher:AES,256

The selection logic is a set intersection, keeping the largest key size both sides support:

def select_cipher(supported: dict, proposed: dict) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    common_ciphers = set(supported.keys()).intersection(proposed.keys())
    cipher, key_size = None, -1
    for c in common_ciphers:
        size = max({-1} | (set(supported[c]) & set(proposed[c])))
        if size > key_size:
            cipher, key_size = c, size
    if not cipher or key_size == -1:
        raise ValueError("Could not agree on a cipher")
    return cipher, key_size

2. Diffie-Hellman key exchange

Each side generates a private value and sends g^x mod p. Each then raises the other's public value to its own private exponent and arrives at the same shared secret, without that secret ever crossing the wire. I used the diffiehellman package, which by default uses the 8192-bit MODP group from RFC 3526 and returns the SHA-256 hex digest of the shared secret.

client → DHMKE:
server → DHMKE:

The cipher key and initialization vector (IV) are then carved out of that digest: the key from the front, the IV from the back.

key = shared_key[:key_size // 8].encode()          # first N characters
iv = shared_key[-ivlen[cipher_name]:].encode()      # last 16 (AES) or 8 characters

3. Authenticated messages

The client pads each message to the block size, encrypts it in CBC mode, and appends an HMAC-SHA256 over the ciphertext. The server recomputes the HMAC and rejects the message if it differs.

ciphertext = crypto.encrypt(add_padding(message))   # AES-CBC
hashing.update(ciphertext)
send(ciphertext + hashing.hexdigest().encode())      # ciphertext || HMAC

Encrypting first and then authenticating the ciphertext is the right construction: it lets the receiver discard a tampered message without decrypting it. The server in this repository doesn't take advantage of that, though; it decrypts first and checks the HMAC second (flaw 6 below).

What this gets right

  • Encrypt-then-MAC. The MAC covers the ciphertext rather than the plaintext, which is the construction that, applied correctly, rules out padding-oracle attacks.
  • No secrets on the wire. The key is derived from Diffie-Hellman rather than shipped or hard-coded.
  • A large, standard group. The default group is an RFC 3526 prime, not a homemade one.

What would break it

Re-reading this code years later, these are the issues I would flag in a review, roughly in order of severity.

  1. No authentication of the peers. Unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle: an attacker on the path can run one exchange with the client and another with the server, then relay and read everything. Real protocols sign the exchange with a long-term key or certificate (TLS), or bind it to static keys known in advance (WireGuard).
  2. A downgrade attack on negotiation. The cipher list is sent in plaintext and is never authenticated later. An attacker can strip AES from the proposal and force the weakest common option. The server in the repository only offers 56-bit DES, which is breakable with modest resources. TLS 1.3 prevents downgrades by including a hash of the entire handshake transcript in the final Finished messages.
  3. Low-entropy keys. The key is taken from the hex string of the digest, so each byte carries 4 bits of entropy instead of 8. An "AES-256" key built this way contains at most 128 bits of entropy. A key-derivation function such as HKDF should expand the shared secret into raw key bytes instead.
  4. The same key for encryption and MAC. Both the cipher and the HMAC use the same key. Separate keys, derived from the shared secret with different labels, are standard practice.
  5. Predictable IVs. The first IV is derived from the shared secret. Every later message continues the CBC chain from the previous ciphertext block, so each message's IV is known before it is encrypted. Predictable IVs were the weakness the BEAST attack exploited in TLS 1.0. CBC needs a fresh, unpredictable IV per message; a modern design would use an AEAD mode such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 with a per-message nonce.
  6. Decrypt before verify. The server decrypts a message before checking its HMAC. With an encrypt-then-MAC scheme, the MAC should be verified first, in constant time, and the message dropped before any decryption happens. The comparison here is also an ordinary string ==, which can leak timing information; hmac.compare_digest exists for this.
  7. No replay protection. Messages carry no sequence number, so a captured message can be re-sent. The rolling HMAC state makes naive replays fail, but only incidentally, and it also means a single dropped message desynchronizes the session.
  8. Ambiguous padding and framing. Messages are padded with null bytes that are stripped on receipt, so a message that legitimately ends in \0 is altered. Messages are also framed by single recv(4096) calls, which assumes TCP preserves message boundaries; it does not.
  9. An unmaintained crypto library. pycrypto has been abandoned since 2013 and has known vulnerabilities. Its maintained successors are pycryptodome and cryptography.

What I took away

Each of the flaws above maps onto a feature that real protocols treat as mandatory: peer authentication, transcript binding, key derivation, key separation, nonces, verify-before-decrypt, sequence numbers, and explicit framing. Building a version without them made it clear why each one exists. A handshake that works is a long way from one that is secure, and most of the engineering lives in the gap.

Built for Luther College's CS-460, Information Assurance and Security (2019–20). The protocol specification and scaffolding came from the course; the implementation is mine.

entry.title: Hello, World
entry.content:
The obligatory first post.

print("Hello, World!")

This is where I'll keep notes on what I'm building and learning: systems, side projects, and the occasional fix for a problem that took longer than it should have.
